notes.2a: This part was generally answered well, although a few candidates described physical rather than chemical properties and could not be credited.
notes.2b: In comparison to (a) this was not well-answered. Many candidates did not recognise the precipitate as Ni(OH) , and few gave balanced equations.
notes.2c: This part showed a clear distinction between candidates familiar with chemical calculations and those less so, with some attempting the calculation without determining the M value of Ni-DMG.
notes.3b: (i) Although this was often well-understood, the use of E° data both here and in (a) was not common.
notes.3bii: Lots of candidates failed to score here because they made no comparison with PbCl .
notes.3c: (i) This scored well, with lots of candidates gaining full marks, although some showed 6 electrons in the outer shell of carbon.
notes.3cii: Most candidates were able to write a balanced equation. �PAGE�35
notes.4a: Most candidates correctly stated ‘hydrogen bonding’, but fewer were able to draw acceptable diagrams, and a significant number showed H-bonds to water.
notes.4b: Many candidates were aware that propylamine was the more basic, but only a small proportion were able to explain why, and a large number failed to include the lone pair on nitrogen in their answers.
notes.4c: Although a good number of candidates wrote acceptable equations, a worrying number failed to give an equation that showed they understood Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases.
notes.4d: (i) A significant number of candidates did not recognise what the intermediate was.
notes.4dii: There are still a significant number of candidates who think that HCN is the reagent here.
notes.4e: This was generally well-answered although some candidates confused the structures of the two compounds and muddled the tests.
notes.5: Overall this was the lowest scoring question on the paper. Candidates showed the usual confusion in using E° data which resulted in a number of lost marks. Candidates also lacked a detailed knowledge of how to use concentration data in cells (learning outcome 6(i)).
notes.5a: (i) A number of candidates used the data for acid solution, or chose one electrode in acid and one in alkaline solution and hence calculated the wrong E . cell
notes.5aii: This was very poorly done with most equations left unbalanced with surplus OH- ions or H O molecules on one or other side of the equation.
notes.5iii: By contrast, equations here were often poor with hydrogen gas being produced.
notes.5iv: A large number of candidates appeared to guess here with extremely few correct explanations.
notes.5v: There were some good answers here in terms of increased rate or better conductivity, but there were a lot of guesses too.
notes.5b: (i) The most common error was to use Eo for Pb4+ rather than for PbO .
notes.5bii: There were a pleasing number of correct equations here.
notes.6a: (i) A pleasing number of candidates managed to identify a suitable reagent.
notes.6aii: Unfortunately not all of those who could give the reagent were able to write a balanced equation for the reaction. �PAGE�36
notes.6b: (i) There were a large number of poor drawings of structures here. Candidates must show the correct atoms bonded in the right sequence or risk penalty. A significant number lost a mark here for showing either oxygen or nitrogen bonded to the ring rather than carbon.
notes.6bii: Most candidates scored at least one of the marks here.
notes.6iii: Very poorly answered with some candidates apparently confusing which way the pH scale runs.
notes.6c: (i) The identification of C and D was generally poor, with candidates ignoring the statement in the stem that both were acyl chlorides.
notes.6cii: This was much more successfully answered, with most candidates knowing that this was hydrogen bonding.
notes.7: This question proved very testing and discriminated well between good and very good candidates. A concern was that a significant number of candidates were not comfortable using skeletal formulae despite their prominence in the syllabus for a number of years now.
notes.8a: This part was well-answered with a significant number of candidates scoring good marks. The most common error (other than spelling) was to confuse the deoxyribose and phosphate.
notes.8c: Again candidates clearly knew the differences between DNA and RNA.
notes.8d: This part was less-well answered with a number of candidates apparently relying on their knowledge from biology and not focusing on the chemical principles.
notes.9a: This was very poorly answered with few candidates scoring both of the marks. Few could adequately explain two spin-states for a proton and a large number omitted to mention any external magnetic field.
notes.9b: This was again poorly answered, with a significant number of candidates reading ‘relative areas’ to mean ‘relative positions’. Even so, when they used the Data Booklet they gave values for absorptions that were not present in the spectrum shown.
notes.9c: (i) Answers here were very disappointing with many candidates unable to draw correct structures for the named compounds. In some cases they even failed to draw compounds that were isomers of one another.
notes.9cii: For reasons that are unclear, a number of candidates seemed to think that peaks A and B came from different compounds and did not refer back to the spectrum they had been given.
notes.9d: (i) Candidates were generally not clear in what information they thought that X-ray crystallography could provide and some merely repeated what was stated in the question.
notes.9dii: Although most candidates knew that this was hydrogen, there was a range of incorrect answers that suggested this may not have been taught to all candidates. �PAGE�37
notes.10a: It was expected from the stem of this question that candidates would think about acid hydrolysis and hence give ester or amide (or possibly nitrile) as the answer. A significant number incorrectly gave alcohol or amine as answers.
notes.10b: This was very poorly answered with candidates often ignoring the instruction to circle bonds and circling individual atoms instead. Those who followed the instructions sometimes circled C=O or – OH bonds incorrectly.
notes.10c: (i) This was generally well-answered with candidates correctly identifying hydrophilic and hydrophobic environments within the liposome.
notes.10cii: Once again there were some good answers here, but some of those who scored the mark in the earlier part were unclear about the reason why position A was unsatisfactory.
notes.10d: (i) Despite the limited choices available, a significant number of candidates failed to score this easy mark.
notes.10dii: Candidates did not seem to take into account the likely relative sizes of a PEG molecule compared with a liposome, in particular the volume of the latter and the two different environments present.
notes.10e: Answers here were generally sensible and, in the main, were based on scientific logic. �PAGE�38
notes.general_comments:
This paper provided candidates of all abilities the opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge and
understanding of a wide range of Chemistry. Candidates who were well-prepared for the examination were
able to tackle all of the questions. There was no evidence that candidates had insufficient time to complete
the paper.
